strengths: The paper addresses a practical stitching problem with a sensible strategy: identify unreliable seam segments and repair their local alignment. The curb and staircase examples show convincing reductions in visible discontinuities.

Evaluation covers 79 image pairs across three datasets, including two public datasets. The proposed method receives 108 of 160 first-place votes in the user study, supporting its perceptual benefit on the selected examples.
The high-level pipeline is understandable, reused methods and public datasets are cited, and key parameters are reported. Section 4.4 and Fig. 12 provide useful, candid discussion of failure cases.
weaknesses: The incremental contribution is insufficiently isolated. Seam evaluation follows [17], correspondence estimation uses SIFT flow [20], and seam-guided alignment already appears in [18]. The specific contribution is the localized flow modification and reinsertion, but beyond the single-patch illustration in Fig. 4, systematic ablations do not establish the value of the sigmoid modification, patch-selection strategy, or parameter choices.

Dataset-wide quantitative comparisons cover only seam-cutting methods [16,17], which retain the initial alignment, whereas the proposed method adds alignment refinement. These comparisons demonstrate the benefit of additional warping but provide limited evidence of an advance over competing alignment strategies. Comparisons with seam-driven methods [18,26] are restricted to selected visual examples; relevant cited work such as large-parallax alignment [12] is not evaluated.

The sole quantitative quality metric averages the same SSIM signal used to guide repairs. It measures local seam agreement but does not assess geometric distortion or artifacts elsewhere in the mosaic. The acknowledged disagreement between this metric and the dinosaur example reinforces this limitation. The user study provides complementary evidence, but its eight manually selected cases, unspecified selection protocol, and lack of uncertainty estimates limit generalization.

The central flow modification is not specified precisely enough for reliable reproduction. Equation (4) defines a scalar sigmoid of normalized horizontal position, while the modified displacement is written as f(V_i). The actual vector transformation, treatment of other seam orientations, and handling of overlapping repair patches are unclear. Boundary label constraints alone also do not establish geometric continuity when warped patches are reinserted.

The claim of almost removing the rough-alignment assumption exceeds the demonstrated scope. Sections 3.4 and 4.4 still require locally manageable residual displacement and a mostly satisfactory initial seam. Moreover, the test max(Q) <= 1.5 mean(Q) can classify a uniformly high-error seam as plausible, and Algorithm 1 contains no post-repair quality verification. These concerns leave broad reliability under large parallax insufficiently supported.
